a-popular-account-of-dr-livingstone-s-ex:
David Livingstone gives a popular account of his expedition to the Zambesi and its tributaries from 1858 to 1864, as the title page of the 1894 John Murray edition states. He dedicates the book to Lord Palmerston, praising his policy against the slave trade on Africa's west coast and urging the same care for the east. His brother Charles served under him on the expedition.

The narrative follows the river past rapids and fever country, the discovery of Lakes Shirwa and Nyassa, and dealings with the peoples along the banks. Livingstone reports honestly on the expedition's failures, including the death of his wife, Mary. The book is both exploration record and argument for opening Africa to lawful trade.
addison-analysis-of-the-report-of-the-co:
Analysis of the Report of the Committee of the Virginia Assembly, published in 1800 by Alexander Addison, is an American political pamphlet of the early republic. Its subject is a report of a committee of the Virginia Assembly, written on the proceedings of several other states. Those states had sent answers to Virginia's resolutions, and the committee's report judged their replies.

Addison takes that report apart point by point, in the heated argument over states' answers to Virginia that followed the resolutions of the late 1790s. The pamphlet is a piece of the first great American debate about federal power and state protest. It preserves the reasoning of a Federalist-era judge writing for the public in a pamphlet war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-tomb:
An altar tomb is an oblong tomb or monument over a grave, covered with a slab or table resembling an altar. Its oblong form follows the grave beneath, the slab closing the monument like an altar table. The table may stand bare or carry one or more recumbent sculptured figures. It may stand free with all four sides exposed, or with one side against the wall.

Where one side meets the wall, a canopy or niche often rises above it. Free-standing examples show the monument from every side, while wall examples gain their canopy as a frame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-ferdina: A 1913 entry on Ferdinand de Géramb — the Trappist baron. Edmond Obrecht tells his romantic tale. He left the world for La Trappe. The cloister tamed the soldier. A nobleman turned monk. His Pilgrimage charmed the readers. His habit was the Trappist white.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-education-of-: This 1913 reference article on the education of the deaf and dumb — the silent ones' schooling. Ferdinand Moeller unfolds its charitable history. The sign language opened the mind. The schools taught the useful crafts. The apostolate of the deaf children. Its Abbé de l'Épée is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste: A 1913 entry on Nothomb — the Belgian statesman. Pierre Marique notes his London treaties. His pen secured the young kingdom. The nation bless the prudent name. The nineteenth century knew his skill. His 1881 death is famed. His 1839 treaties are famed. His 1839 Belgian treaties are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paschal-lamb: The Paschal Lamb was the lamb of the first Passover, whose blood saved Israel and prefigured Christ. This entry examines its ritual, its meaning, and its fulfillment. The lamb that pointed to the Lamb: its blood marked the doors of Israel.
doe-osti-3383025-complete-the-design-cos: Packed beds got design-costed, and this DOE text completes tubular designs. The pages detail the estimate findings. The engineers get their data. The instructions were operating. The data were engineer. The packed-bed were tubular. The bench-scale were operating.
govdocs-archive_org-ifePhilipTheNazisBig:
Philip Rife wrote The Nazis' Big Apple A-Bomb for the March/April 2013 issue of the Barnes Review. His claim is a large one: that Germany possessed nuclear weapons during the Second World War and planned to bomb New York with them.

Rife assembles testimony, documents, and inference to argue that the German bomb program went far beyond the failed effort described in standard histories. Mainstream historians hold that Germany never came close to a bomb, so the article stands as revisionist military history. It is presented as an archive holding, without endorsement, for readers of that debate.
memoirs-of-lady-fanshawe-wife-of-sir-ric:
Ann Fanshawe wrote the memoirs of her husband, Sir Richard Fanshawe. He served Charles II as envoy to Portugal and Madrid. Beatrice Marshall edited this edition, with a note on its pictures.

The intro praises the mid 1600s as a time of charm and storm. Civil war, a king's trial, and the throne restored fill that span. Fanshawe wrote late in life, for her one son who lived to manhood. Fourteen children were born to her, and most died young abroad. Most of those children rest in foreign churchyards, she notes. Loss at home sits beside state craft in her plain tale.
nasa-tm-19640019314-satellite-situation-:
The Space Operations Control Center at Goddard issued this report on June 30, 1964. It is volume four, number twelve of the satellite situation series. Data came from Goddard, NORAD, and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. The table lists each object in orbit with its orbital facts.

Explorer 1, from February 1958, still heads the launch list. Rocket bodies are cataloged beside the satellites they carried. Columns give period, tilt, high point, low point, and radio frequency. Lunik 1 and Pioneer 4 are marked as circling the Sun instead. The issue is a dated snapshot of all that humans had placed in space by mid-1964.
nasa-tm-19640023261-satellite-situation-: Volume four, number fifteen of NASA's satellite situation report series is preserved here. Reports in the series were compiled by Goddard Space Flight Center with NORAD and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. Catalog notes say this issue lists orbit data and transmitting frequencies for satellites then in orbit. The hosted sample preserves only garbled table data with no readable text, so this issue's date and listings cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19660024016-wind-tunnel-investig:
John E Grimaud at Langley tested three lifting reentry shapes in a wind tunnel at Mach 2.91, for this March 1961 memorandum. Angles of attack ran up to ninety degrees. A lifting reentry body glides as it returns, rather than falling like a capsule. It must stay stable across a huge range of attitudes, some of them far from normal flight.

Grimaud measured stability and control for all three shapes. High-angle data are the hard part of such a test program. A shape that misbehaves at high angles could tumble on entry. Comparing three shapes on the same terms let designers pick the soundest line. The study belongs to the first wave of lifting entry research.
nasa-tm-19710022735-aerodynamic-characte:
William J. Monta of the Langley Research Center wrote this August 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2340, on an unusual missile shape. The model had a blunt, flat-faced nose and a body with a triangular cross section. Three fixed fins, a triform tail, provided its stability and control surfaces.

Wind tunnel tests in the Langley Unitary Plan tunnel covered speeds from Mach 1.60 to Mach 2.16 and many roll orientations. Monta varied nose corner radius, fin span, and fin asymmetry meant to produce rolling moment. Results show the model tended to pitch up in the flat-top orientation and pitch down in the flat-bottom one. A smaller nose corner radius mainly raised axial force, while a larger fin span moved the aerodynamic center rearward.
the-best-letters-of-charles-lamb:
Edward Gilpin Johnson edited a selection of Charles Lamb's letters in 1892, under a heading calling them laurel-crowned. Praise from A. C. Swinburne and W. C. Hazlitt stands at the front. Hazlitt claims no kindred collection matches the letters in range, period, or typical character.

Contents list letter after letter to Samuel Taylor Coleridge, eighteen in the opening run alone. Robert Southey follows as the next named recipient. The order shows Lamb's early writing life bound up with Coleridge. Readers get a famed essayist in private form, writing to poet friends rather than to the public of his Essays of Elia.
the-secret-tomb: Maurice Le Blanc's The Secret Tomb was copyrighted by The Macaulay Company in New York in 1923. Le Blanc is billed as creator of Arsene Lupin. George W. Gage supplied the frontispiece. The pages shown give the title matter and the start of the contents only. The Château de Roborey opens the list. Dorothy's circus, extra lucid, and a cross-examination follow. We will help you is promised in chapter five. No story text appears here.
the-uphill-climb: B. M. Bower, author of Good Indian and Chip, of the Flying U, published The Uphill Climb with Grosset and Dunlap in 1913. Charles M. Russell illustrated the western. The pages present here hold the title page, a seventeen-chapter contents list, and an illustrations list, but no story text. Chapter one is titled Married! And I Don't Know Her Name. Later headings follow Ford through reaction, a plan gone wrong, and a fight with the Demon. Closing titles promise a climb and a search to free a wife.
the-wolves-and-the-lamb:
William Makepeace Thackeray's The Wolves and the Lamb is a play set at a villa in Richmond. The cast lists Horace Milliken, a wealthy widowed merchant. His mother-in-law, Lady Kicklebury, figures prominently. A governess, Miss Prior, cares for the Milliken children. Servants, a captain, and the Bonningtons round out the household.

Act one opens in two adjoining drawing rooms. The late Mrs. Milliken's portrait hangs over the mantelpiece. Bookcases, a piano, and newspapers furnish the rooms. Large windows look onto a lawn and pleasure ground. Thackeray sets a comfortable home where sharp social maneuvering can unfold.
universite-de-paris-faculte-de-theologie:
The Faculty of Theology of Paris addressed these humble petitions to the French king in 1730. Their grievance was a ruling by the Parlement, handed down on May 17 of that year, against a theology thesis defended on May 8 by a licentiate named Hassett. Bound with the petitions is the reply letter of the Comte de Maurepas, a secretary of state, written by order of the king.

The faculty open with thanks for recent royal favors, then say duty forces them to mix sorrow with gratitude. They argue that the ruling struck at their rights and honor, since the thesis had passed under their own authority. The French text keeps the old spelling and formal address of court papers of the time. Readers get a close look at a church faculty defending its turf against a royal court of law.
